text:
Broccoli.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn / Winter

Calabrese produces a green central head in summer or autumn, followed by smaller side shoots. Sprouting broccoli stands through winter and gives tender purple or white spears when other greens are scarce. Choose the type for the season you want to harvest.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jan – May; Jul – Oct

Germination

7–12 days

Sowing depth

3/4 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between seed rows

Yield per plant

1 1/2 lb

Ready in

Calabrese ~12 weeks; sprouting ~44 weeks from sowing

Sow

Calabrese indoors Mar or outdoors May–late Jun. Sprouting types Apr for large plants or Jun for smaller ones.

Plant spacing

Sprouting: 30 in. between plants and rows; calabrese: 12–18 in. between plants, rows 18 in. apart

Transplant

Early calabrese Apr under fleece. Sprouting broccoli Jun–Jul.

Recommended varieties
PURPLE SPROUTING
Early Purple Sprouting

An overwintering broccoli producing purple shoots in spring. Allow it a long growing season and pick the shoots regularly.

CALABRESE
Green Magic F1

An early calabrese producing a dense central head followed by side shoots. A practical choice for a summer broccoli crop.

PURPLE SPROUTING
Claret F1

A purple-sprouting broccoli for a later spring harvest. Useful for extending cropping beyond earlier sprouting varieties.

CALABRESE
Marathon F1

A dependable summer calabrese with firm blue-green heads. A useful alternative to Green Magic for the main crop.

Key risks
Cabbage caterpillars

Summer and autumn broccoli is very prone to caterpillar damage.

Club root (finger and toe)

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather.

Frost

Sprouting broccoli is winter-hardy, but severe frost can damage shoots.

Pigeons

Pigeons can strip young plants and winter crops.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
28
BRASSICAS

Choose a sunny site.

Prepare in autumn, adding compost or well-rotted manure if soil is poor.

Firm the planting ground.

Do not leave brassica soil loose and fluffy before transplanting.

Water and mulch in dry weather.

Feed crops that are growing poorly.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, firm, fertile soil. Prepare in autumn with compost or well-rotted manure if soil is poor; lime only if needed.
Firm the settled bed before planting. Sprouting broccoli can follow peas, beans, garlic, early roots or salads if the ground is ready in time.
Sowing & planting
Raise seedlings
Transplant firmly
Sow 

Scatter seed thinly in a nursery row or put two seeds in each module. Thin modules to one seedling. Raise early calabrese under cover.

Transplant 

Lift sturdy seedlings with soil around their roots. Harden off plants raised under cover. Set the lowest leaves just above the soil, firm well and water. Sprouting broccoli needs more room than calabrese.

Looking after the crop
Hoe regularly. Mesh guards against caterpillars, especially on late calabrese. Hold bird netting clear of leaves so pigeons cannot peck through.
Water in dry weather and mulch in summer. Use an organic liquid feed if growth is weak.
Stake tall sprouting plants on exposed sites; mulch with straw in very cold winters.
Check for club root and caterpillars. Hand-pick pests and remove damaged or diseased leaves.
Harvesting & storage
Cut formed calabrese heads before buds open or stems elongate, protecting surrounding leaves. Side shoots follow in 2–3 weeks; steady growth can extend picking to about two months.
Late calabrese may crop into autumn or early winter, but drought reduces yield and frost damages buds.
Pick the main sprouting spear first, then tender side shoots regularly. Early sorts may start in January in mild seasons; late sorts reach April–May. Later shoots become thinner and more numerous as plants try to flower.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Cabbage caterpillars	Chewed leaves; caterpillars.	Pick off eggs and caterpillars; cover with fine mesh.
Club root (finger and toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Frost	Cold-damaged shoots.	Firm loosened plants; stake exposed stems and mulch.
Pigeons	Leaves pecked or stripped.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Cabbage root fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Fit collars or insect-proof mesh; rotate brassicas.
Slugs and snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; remove yellow leaves around seedlings.
Final tips

Side shoots follow the main calabrese head.

Keep netting clear of leaves.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
